851.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
851.explanation: The Jain passions (kaṣāyas) are presented as forces that eat away at the bonds between beings, with anger first destroying love.
851.tie_back: Valluvar calls hostility a disease that breeds separation in every creature, and the Jain verse likewise makes the passions destroyers of love and friendship, the very bonds hostility breaks.
851.source: Saman Suttam v. 135 (Samyamasūtra; drawn from Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
851._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Saman Suttam Samyamasūtra page on jainworld.com. It is about anger and the other passions rather than hostility (ikal) as such, and it lacks the Kural's 'disease' metaphor.

852.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry. … A monk should not be angry if beaten, nor should he therefore entertain sinful thoughts; knowing patience to be the highest good, a monk should meditate on the Law.”
852.explanation: Among the troubles a monk must bear, being abused and being struck are to be met with patience and without any thought of retaliation, since patience is the highest good.
852.tie_back: The Kural says that even when someone deliberately does you harm, the highest course is not to strike back in hostility, and Mahavira's rule for abuse and blows says the same.
852.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.24 and 2.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
852._accuracy_note: Both verses checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; verse 2.25 is left out at the ellipsis. A near-direct match, though it is framed as monastic discipline rather than general conduct.

853.quote_or_event: In Hemacandra's life of Pārśvanātha, Kamaṭha nurses a hatred for his brother Marubhūti that lasts through many births. In the last of them, as the god Meghamālin, he attacks the meditating Pārśva with storm and flood, while Pārśva never answers with hostility. The Kalpa Sūtra gives Pārśva the lasting epithet 'the people's favourite' (puruṣādānīya).
853.explanation: Jain tradition contrasts the enemy whose rage drags him through birth after birth with the Tīrthaṅkara who, free of enmity, becomes the most beloved and honoured of teachers.
853.tie_back: The Kural promises unfading renown to whoever rids himself of the disease of hostility, and Pārśva, who never returned Kamaṭha's enmity, is remembered with a lasting title of affection.
853.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book IX (Pārśvanāthacaritra), tr. Helen M. Johnson; Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Pārśva (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
853._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested story, confirmed this session only through wisdomlib summaries and search snippets, not the full Johnson chapter; the 'people's favourite' epithet was likewise confirmed by search. Linking Pārśva's renown to his freedom from enmity is an interpretive bridge the texts do not state outright.

854.quote_or_event: “By begging forgiveness he obtains happiness of mind; thereby he acquires a kind disposition towards all kinds of living beings; by this kind disposition he obtains purity of character and freedom from fear.”
854.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana traces a chain of fruits from the practice of asking forgiveness (kṣamāpana): first happiness of mind, then goodwill toward all beings, then purity and freedom from fear.
854.tie_back: Valluvar says that once hostility, the sorrow of sorrows, is destroyed, it yields the joy of joys, and the Jain text likewise makes happiness of mind the first fruit of ending hostility through forgiveness.
854.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
854._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). It matches the turn from hostility to happiness well, but it does not use the Kural's superlative 'joy of joys' contrast.

855.quote_or_event: “They indeed had no effect whatever on the Lord whose power was great. Is a wind, even great, able to shake Meru?”
855.explanation: The furious serpent Caṇḍakauśika burns Mahavira with its poisonous gaze and bites him again and again. The Lord stays unmoved and without hostility, and the serpent, overcome by his calm, gives up its anger altogether.
855.tie_back: The Kural asks who could ever defeat those who turn away from hostility, and Caṇḍakauśika's venom cannot even shake Mahavira, who wins not by fighting back but by staying free of enmity.
855.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. III, part 10 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
855._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Johnson translation on wisdomlib.org. A strong narrative match for the one who cannot be overcome because he does not answer hostility, though it is told of a Jina's extraordinary power.

856.quote_or_event: “He stumbled and fell into a pit that was like the mouth of hell. As he fell, the sharp axe fell on him and split his head in two. For there was maturing of bad karma.”
856.explanation: In a former birth, the hot-tempered ascetic Kauśika rushes with an axe at men breaking into his woods. His own fury throws him into a pit, where his own axe kills him, and the text adds that anger carries on into the next birth.
856.tie_back: The Kural warns that for whoever thinks it sweet to get ahead through hostility, failure and ruin are close at hand, and Kauśika's charge ends in his destruction within moments.
856.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. III, part 10 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
856._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Johnson translation on wisdomlib.org. A vivid instance of hostility bringing swift ruin; it is a single story rather than a general maxim, and it comes from the same episode used for 855.

857.quote_or_event: After his duel with his brother Bharata, Bāhubali renounces the kingdom and stands so long in motionless meditation that vines grow over him. Yet omniscience (kevala-jñāna) does not come until his sisters Brāhmī and Sundarī tell him to get down from the elephant, meaning the pride left over from the rivalry. Once he lets it go, he attains omniscience.
857.explanation: Jain tradition uses Bāhubali to show that even immense austerity cannot reveal the highest truth while a trace of passion born of rivalry remains in the mind.
857.tie_back: The Kural says that minds attached to hostility can never see the true principle, and Bāhubali, rival of his brother, cannot reach omniscience until the last remnant of that rivalry is gone.
857.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (Ādīśvaracaritra), tr. Helen M. Johnson; widely retold in Śvetāmbara tradition
857._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known story, confirmed this session through search results and wisdomlib listings rather than the full Johnson chapter. In most tellings the obstacle is pride (māna) rather than hostility as such, so the match is partial.

858.quote_or_event: “A cruel man does cruel acts and is thereby involved in other cruelties; but sinful undertakings will in the end bring about misery.”
858.explanation: Jacobi's note glosses the 'cruel man' (Prakrit vêri, Sanskrit vairin) as one who is hostile and hurts living beings. The verse teaches that such enmity drags a person into further enmity and ends in misery.
858.tie_back: Valluvar says that whoever pushes hostility further invites ruin to hurry toward him, and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga describes the same spiral: the hostile man's cruelties breed more cruelties and end in misery.
858.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
858._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com, including his footnote glossing vêri as vairin. A good fit for hostility escalating toward ruin, but it has no counterpart to the Kural's first line, where turning away from hostility brings prosperity.

859.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
859.explanation: The lecture on impurity warns that wealth gained wrongly is lost once a person falls under the power of his passions and hatred.
859.tie_back: The Kural ties a person's rising or falling fortune to whether he ignores or magnifies hostility, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise links losing one's wealth to being held captive by hatred.
859.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
859._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It shares the link between hatred and lost prosperity, but its focus is on wrongly acquired wealth, and it does not contain the Kural's idea that hostility is a symptom of fortune already turning.

860.quote_or_event: “I forgive all living beings and may all living beings forgive me; I cherish feelings of friendship towards all and I harbour enmity towards none.”
860.explanation: This verse, recited in the Jain rite of forgiveness (Khāmemi savva jīve), pairs friendship (metti) toward all beings with enmity (vera) toward none as the heart of the religious life.
860.tie_back: The Kural's closing couplet sets hostility, the source of all painful things, against friendliness, the source of true good, and the Jain verse makes the same pairing of friendship toward all and enmity toward none.
860.source: Saman Suttam v. 86 (Dharmasūtra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com); Prakrit 'Khammāmi savvajīvāṇaṃ … mittī me savvabhūdesu, veraṃ majjhaṃ na keṇa vi'
860._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Saman Suttam Dharmasūtra page on jainworld.com. It mirrors the Kural's opposition of enmity and friendship, but it is a vow of attitude rather than a statement of their consequences.
